Francisco Cafiero, a former secretary for international relations at the defense ministry, said the episode reflected a broader lack of strategic clarity. "Here, we navigate amidst uncertainty and improvisation," he said.

item.title: John Eastman asks US Supreme Court to undo disbarment over Trump election efforts
item.description: Conservative attorney John Eastman has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to reinstate his California law license after he was disbarred in the state earlier this year over his efforts to overturn Republican President Donald Trump's 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
item.dc:creator: David Thomas
item.content:encoded: Conservative attorney John Eastman has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to reinstate his California law license after he was [USN:L1N3XG14E TEXT:"disbarred in the state "][USN:L1N3XG14E TEXT:"earlier this year"] over his efforts to overturn Republican President Donald Trump's 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Eastman said in a petition to the high court filed on Friday that his legal advocacy was protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, and that he was disciplined in a "politicized" bar proceeding. He said other attorneys who took part in legal proceedings that sought to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election were not disciplined. "While states may regulate genuine attorney misconduct, they may not use disciplinary authority to punish protected advocacy by relabeling it as professional misconduct," the petition said. Eastman is represented in the Supreme Court petition by Jay Sekulow, another former lawyer for Trump. Sekulow did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It is rare for the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on attorney disciplinary cases, which are normally decided by the top court of respective states. A former law professor at Chapman University in California, Eastman had represented Trump in a long-shot lawsuit at the U.S. Supreme Court that sought to invalidate votes in four states where the Republican former president had falsely claimed evidence of widespread voter fraud in the 2020 US presidential election. Eastman had also drafted legal memos weeks after the election suggesting then-Vice President Mike Pence could refuse to accept electoral votes from several swing states when Congress convened to certify the vote count. Pence had rebuffed his arguments, saying he did not have the legal authority to do so under the U.S. Constitution. Eastman repeated many of his election claims at a rally outside the White House on January 6, 2021, after which a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol and delayed congressional certification of the election. A judge on California's State Bar Court had recommended Eastman's disbarment in March 2024, [USN:L1N3DD2S9 TEXT:"determining"] that his efforts to derail Biden's victory were "unlawful and lacked any factual or legal support." Eastman's law license was suspended as he appealed the finding. The State Bar Court's appellate division had [USN:L1N3SE0RM TEXT:"last year found"] that Eastman violated California attorney ethics rules against misleading courts and making false public statements. The California Supreme Court denied Eastman's petition for review. Eastman had argued to the bar court's Review Department that his rights to free speech and due process were violated by state bar prosecutors, and complained that he was singled out for punishment by the judge who heard his case.

item.title: EU is set to propose ban on social media and AI chatbots for under-15s
item.description: The European Union will propose a ban restricting under 15s from social media, video sharing platforms, AI chatbots and online games, in the most sweeping plan yet to protect children from online dangers, a European Commission document seen by Reuters shows.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: The European Union will propose a ban restricting under 15s from social media, video sharing platforms, AI chatbots and online games, in the most sweeping plan yet to protect children from online dangers, a European Commission document seen by Reuters shows. Concerns have mounted globally about the impact on children's [USN:L6N44N0VA TEXT:"health and safety"] of major outlets, including Meta's (META.O) Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google's (GOOGL.O) YouTube and ChatGPT. The EU proposal is part of an EU Kids Act that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen will present on Thursday. The former may announce some details in her State of the Union address on upcoming EU policy on Wednesday. "The Union's approach should allow minors to benefit from the huge potential of digital services, while protecting them from abuse and exploitation. It needs to limit the access of tech companies to our children, and not the other way around," the document said. The Commission's proposal, which will also cover video gaming platforms, allows for gradual access to the various services according to age, while the obligations imposed on the companies will depend on the type of service and the age of the children. The Commission declined to comment. COMPANIES WOULD HAVE TO PAY A SUPERVISORY FEE According to the document, companies will have to pay a supervisory fee to fund regulators' enforcement and supervision. Children from 15 onwards can set up their own accounts under the proposal, while children between 13 and 14 can ask parents to open introductory accounts for social media and video-sharing platforms under parental control and with limited contacts and strict time limits. Accounts for children between 3 and 12 will be fully controlled by parents and will only be for child-friendly services with strict safety standards, the document said. Under-3s would have no access to the services. Details may still change ahead of the announcement. The Commission will need to work out the draft with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law. The draft seen by Reuters sets out requirements for companies, including avoiding addictive designs and harmful feeds. They would also have to provide tools to enable children to easily report harmful content and effective parental control tools. Social media and video-sharing platforms will be required to verify children's age when a user opens a new account while online games platforms will have to verify children's age before they can download games. The companies say they take precautions and many set a minimum age of [USN:L6N44L075 TEXT:"at least 13"] to sign up to social media platforms.

item.title: Juíza dos EUA diz que permanecerá no caso contra OpenAI após vender ações da Microsoft
item.description: A juíza federal Ona Wang, que supervisiona as questões pré-julgamento em um processo histórico sobre direitos autorais movido por autores e veículos de comunicação, incluindo o New York Times contra a OpenAI e seu maior financiador, a Microsoft , revelou em um documento judicial em Manhattan na sexta-feira que possuía ações da Microsoft, mas não se declararia impedida de participar do caso.
item.dc:creator: Blake Brittain
item.content:encoded: A juíza federal Ona Wang, que supervisiona as questões pré-julgamento em um processo histórico sobre direitos autorais movido por autores e veículos de comunicação, incluindo o New York Times (NYT.N) contra a OpenAI e seu maior financiador, a Microsoft (MSFT.O) , revelou em um documento judicial em Manhattan na sexta-feira que possuía ações da Microsoft, mas não se declararia impedida de participar do caso. Wang afirmou no processo que, embora as normas judiciais normalmente exigissem seu afastamento, ela havia vendido a sua participação na empresa e que isso não havia afetado nenhuma de suas decisões. A juíza também afirmou que continuar supervisionando o caso seria de interesse público para "evitar que o assunto fosse reatribuído a outromagistrado". Representantes da Microsoft, da OpenAI e do The New York Times não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentários sobre o processo nesta segunda-feira. Um porta-voz do tribunal de Wang, o Tribunal Distrital dos EUA para o Distrito Sul de Nova York, e um advogado dos autores recusaram-se a comentar. O processo movido pelo The Times, inicialmente apresentado em 2023, acusa a OpenAI e a Microsoft de usar milhões de artigos de jornais sem permissão para treinar o ChatGPT. Os autores, entre os quais John Grisham, Jonathan Franzen e George RR Martin, processaram separadamente as empresas no mesmo ano por utilizarem seus livros para treinar o popular chatbot da OpenAI. Esses casos e ações judiciais relacionadas contra a OpenAI foram consolidados em Nova York no ano passado. Dezenas de outras queixas também foram apresentadas por detentores de direitos autorais contra empresas de tecnologia pelo que consideram o roubo de seu material para treinar sistemas de IA. (Reportagem de Blake Brittain em Washington)

item.title: Report: Cowboys S Malik Hooker to see specialist for forearm fracture
item.description: Dallas Cowboys safety Malik Hooker has been diagnosed with a forearm fracture and is scheduled to meet with a specialist to determine a recovery timeline, ESPN reported Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Dallas Cowboys safety Malik Hooker has been diagnosed with a forearm fracture and is scheduled to meet with a specialist to determine a recovery timeline, ESPN reported Monday. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said after Sunday's game that a fractured forearm was a possibility. Hooker was injured during Sunday night's 28-20 road loss to the New York Giants when he stumbled to the ground and got caught up with Giants tight end Chris Manhertz late in the third quarter. To start his 10th NFL season, Hooker had one tackle while playing 12 defensive snaps in the season opener. In 113 career games (89 starts), he has 414 tackles with 14 interceptions and 25 passes defended for the Indianapolis Colts (2017-20) and Cowboys. Hooker was a first-round draft pick (15th overall) by the Colts in 2017 out of Ohio State. --Field Level Media

item.title: Câmara Alta do Parlamento suíço aprova acordo comercial com Mercosul
item.description: A Câmara Alta do Parlamento da Suíça aprovou nesta segunda-feira um acordo comercial com o Mercosul, após prometer apoio aos agricultores suíços, reenviando o acordo à Câmara Baixa, onde havia sido rejeitado em junho.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Câmara Alta do Parlamento da Suíça aprovou nesta segunda-feira um acordo comercial com o Mercosul, após prometer apoio aos agricultores suíços, reenviando o acordo à Câmara Baixa, onde havia sido rejeitado em junho. Um ano após o ministro da Economia da Suíça ter assinado o acordo no Brasil, os parlamentares da Câmara Alta aprovaram o acordo juntamente com um auxílio financeiro aos agricultores no valor de 517 milhões de francos suíços (US$633 milhões) ao longo de seis anos para amenizar seu impacto. O acordo entre os Estados-membros da Associação Europeia de Livre Comércio (EFTA) e o núcleo do Mercosul — formado por Argentina, Brasil, Paraguai e Uruguai — foi aprovado com 35 votos a favor e sete contra. Houve três abstenções. A agricultura é uma área política sensível na Suíça, e a oposição ao acordo na Câmara Baixa veio tanto da direita quanto da esquerda do espectro político suíço. A Suíça é a maior economia da EFTA, que também inclui a Noruega, a Islândia e o Liechtenstein. (Reportagem de Dave Graham)

item.title: GRANOS El trigo baja por esperanzas de distensión en el mar Negro; soja y maíz suben
item.description: Los futuros del trigo estadounidense caían el lunes a su nivel más bajo en más de dos semanas por las esperanzas de una distensión del conflicto del mar Negro, mientras que la soja repuntó debido al aumento de los precios de la energía y a la amenaza de retrasos en la cosecha del Medio Oeste, según analistas.
item.dc:creator: Julie Ingwersen
item.content:encoded: Los futuros del trigo estadounidense caían el lunes a su nivel más bajo en más de dos semanas por las esperanzas de una distensión del conflicto del mar Negro, mientras que la soja repuntó debido al aumento de los precios de la energía y a la amenaza de retrasos en la cosecha del Medio Oeste, según analistas. El maíz se consolidó, siguiendo la estela de la soja y tras un alza del crudo, pero el retroceso del trigo limitó las ganancias. A las 1559 GMT, el trigo para diciembre en la Bolsa de Chicago bajaba 3,25 centavos, a 7,22 dólares por bushel, tras caer a 7,10 dólares, un mínimo desde el 26 de agosto. El contrato de soja para noviembre subía 9,50 centavos, a 13,06 dólares por bushel, y el de maíz para diciembre ganaba 2,25 centavos, a 5,3250 dólares por bushel. El trigo retrocedió después de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, dijo que Ucrania y Rusia habían acordado no atacar los objetivos energéticos del otro. "Las posiciones largas de los fondos gestionados parecen interpretar esta renovada presión por parte de EEUU como algo que podría llevar a una distensión en lo que respecta al flujo de materias primas a través del mar Negro, pero solo el tiempo dirá si esto se traduce realmente en una mejora", dijo el analista de StoneX, Mike Castle. Los fondos de gestión de materias primas recortaron ligeramente su posición larga neta en los futuros de trigo de la CBOT durante la semana que finalizó el 8 de septiembre, según datos semanales de las autoridades reguladoras estadounidenses. La soja de la CBOT repuntó tras el débil cierre del viernes, cobrando fuerza a medida que el crudo subía más de un 2% debido a la escalada de tensión en Oriente Medio. El aceite de soja es una materia prima para el biodiésel. Además, las previsiones apuntaban a fuertes lluvias que podrían ralentizar la cosecha en algunas zonas del Medio Oeste esta semana, incluido Iowa, el principal productor agrícola de Estados Unidos y el segundo estado sojero.

item.title: Cámara alta del Parlamento suizo respalda acuerdo comercial con el Mercosur
item.description: La cámara alta del Parlamento suizo aprobó el lunes un acuerdo comercial con el bloque Mercosur, tras prometer apoyo a los agricultores locales, y devolvió el proyecto a la cámara baja, que lo había sido rechazado en junio.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La cámara alta del Parlamento suizo aprobó el lunes un acuerdo comercial con el bloque Mercosur, tras prometer apoyo a los agricultores locales, y devolvió el proyecto a la cámara baja, que lo había sido rechazado en junio. Un año después de que el ministro de Economía suizo firmara el acuerdo en Brasil, los diputados de la cámara alta aprobaron el pacto junto con una ayuda económica para los agricultores por valor de 517 millones de francos suizos (633 millones de dólares) a lo largo de seis años para amortiguar su impacto. El acuerdo entre los Estados miembros de la Asociación Europea de Libre Comercio (AELC) y el núcleo del Mercosur —formado por Argentina, Brasil, Paraguay y Uruguay— se aprobó con 35 votos a favor y siete en contra. Hubo tres abstenciones. La agricultura es un ámbito político delicado en Suiza y la oposición al acuerdo en la Cámara Baja este verano boreal había provenido tanto de los partidos de derecha como de izquierda. Suiza es la mayor economía de la AELC, que también comprende a Noruega, Islandia y Liechtenstein. (1 dólar = 0,8162 francos suizos)

item.title: Senadores de EEUU consideran exigir a gigantes de la IA que se comprometan a prevenir catástrofes
item.description: Los negociadores del Senado de Estados Unidos están debatiendo una ley que obligaría a las empresas de inteligencia artificial a demostrar que están tomando precauciones razonables para evitar que sus herramientas causen daños, según un asesor del Senado y un lobista familiarizados con las conversaciones.
item.dc:creator: Courtney Rozen
item.content:encoded: Los negociadores del Senado de Estados Unidos están debatiendo una ley que obligaría a las empresas de inteligencia artificial a demostrar que están tomando precauciones razonables para evitar que sus herramientas causen daños, según un asesor del Senado y un lobista familiarizados con las conversaciones. La preocupación por los posibles daños derivados de la IA aumentó la semana pasada cuando el investigador de Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, anunció su dimisión, en parte porque "las personas que desarrollan la IA creen sinceramente que podría acabar con todos nosotros antes de que termine la década". Las acciones relacionadas con la IA cayeron en todo el mundo el lunes después de que los jefes de algunas de las mayores empresas del sector pidieron que se ralentizara el ritmo de desarrollo de la tecnología. Los senadores están debatiendo la posibilidad de otorgar al secretario de Comercio de Estados Unidos la facultad de solicitar pruebas de que los desarrolladores de IA están tomando medidas razonables para prevenir daños, lo que se conoce como "deber de diligencia", según el asistente del Senado y el lobista. El secretario también tendría la facultad de enviar a auditores del Gobierno para que prueben ellos mismos los productos de las empresas, agregaron. Reuters no pudo determinar de inmediato qué se consideraría "razonable". La legislación sigue siendo objeto de debate. Incluso si el Congreso aprueba la medida, tiene pocas posibilidades de convertirse en ley. El presidente de Estados , Donald Trump, dijo el lunes que las autoridades existentes ya disponen de herramientas adecuadas para regular y perseguir a las empresas tecnológicas, lo que sugiere que no firmaría un proyecto de ley que estableciera nuevas normas para la IA. La propuesta está siendo debatida por el líder de la mayoría del Senado, John Thune; el presidente de la Comisión de Comercio del Senado, Ted Cruz, y la senadora Amy Klobuchar, la principal representante demócrata que participa en las negociaciones. Los portavoces de Thune y Cruz no respondieron de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentarios de Reuters.

item.title: Homem britânico confessa ter drogado e estuprado esposa por mais de duas décadas
item.description: Um homem britânico admitiu, nesta segunda-feira, ter repetidamente drogado e estuprado sua esposa em casa ao longo de mais de duas décadas, pouco antes do início de seu julgamento.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Um homem britânico admitiu, nesta segunda-feira, ter repetidamente drogado e estuprado sua esposa em casa ao longo de mais de duas décadas, pouco antes do início de seu julgamento. O homem — do norte da Inglaterra, com cerca de 60 anos, mas cujo nome não pode ser divulgado para não identificar sua esposa, que tem direito ao anonimato vitalício — se declarou culpado no Tribunal da Coroa de Minshull Street, em Manchester, de 45 acusações, tendo admitido anteriormente 15 crimes. O homem admitiu agora acusações que incluem 21 crimes de estupro, 15 de agressão com penetração, 11 de agressão sexual e um de compartilhamento de imagens íntimas sem consentimento, no período entre 2004 e 2025. Ele também admitiu ter cometido o crime de administrar uma substância com o objetivo de deixar sua esposa inconsciente. Os promotores afirmam que a mulher foi repetidamente estuprada e agredida sexualmente em sua própria casa enquanto estava inconsciente, após ter sido drogada pelo marido. Outros doze homens, com idades entre 28 e 74 anos, também são acusados de abusar sexualmente da vítima de 2018 a 2025 e todos negaram os crimes, que incluem estupro. “Nosso foco continua sendo apoiar a vítima dessa terrível campanha de abuso ao longo dessa investigação muito complexa”, disse o subchefe da Polícia da Grande Manchester, Rick Jackson. “Continua sendo prestado apoio especializado à vítima que está no centro deste caso.” O julgamento dos outros homens está marcado para ocorrer no mesmo tribunal e deve durar vários meses.

item.title: Enviados de la UE prorrogan sanciones a Rusia por siete días para debatir renovación por seis meses
item.description: Los representantes de la Unión Europea aplazaron siete días la fecha de vencimiento de las listas de sanciones de la UE contra Rusia, al 22 de septiembre, informó el lunes un portavoz de la Presidencia irlandesa de la UE, tras no alcanzar un acuerdo sobre una prórroga de seis meses.
item.dc:creator: Julia Payne
item.content:encoded: Los representantes de la Unión Europea aplazaron siete días la fecha de vencimiento de las listas de sanciones de la UE contra Rusia, al 22 de septiembre, informó el lunes un portavoz de la Presidencia irlandesa de la UE, tras no alcanzar un acuerdo sobre una prórroga de seis meses. La cuestión es si se debe retirar de la lista al multimillonario ruso-uzbeko Alisher Usmanov. Francia se ha sumado a Eslovaquia en su petición de excluirlo, alegando motivos de seguridad nacional, indicaron diplomáticos de la UE. "Francia es uno de los países más comprometidos con aumentar la presión —por todos los medios— sobre la maquinaria bélica rusa, así como con apoyar a Ucrania", dijo una fuente diplomática francesa. "Nos enfrentamos a un problema concreto de seguridad nacional y deseamos responder positivamente a los socios internacionales que se han dirigido a nosotros en relación con el señor Usmanov". El portavoz del Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores de Francia se negó a hacer comentarios. Las sanciones, que afectan a cerca de 3.000 empresas y personas con la congelación de activos y la prohibición de viajar, debían expirar el 15 de septiembre. "Con el fin de conceder más tiempo a los Estados miembros para examinar exhaustivamente las propuestas de renovación, el Coreper ha acordado prorrogar el régimen por un período de siete días, hasta la medianoche del martes 22 de septiembre", dijo el portavoz, refiriéndose al Comité de Representantes Permanentes —el órgano de embajadores de la UE que prepara los trabajos para los 27 jefes de Estado de los Estados miembros. Las sanciones de la UE requieren la aprobación unánime de los 27 Estados miembros y deben renovarse cada seis meses. Según el Índice de Multimillonarios de Bloomberg, Usmanov tenía un patrimonio neto de 18.800 millones de dólares a principios de 2026, y está sujeto a sanciones de la UE y Estados Unidos, así como a una prohibición de viajar. Usmanov, un magnate de la metalurgia y la minería, ha interpuesto múltiples demandas en Europa con el objetivo último de que se levanten las sanciones. En algunas de ellas, sus abogados impugnaron las declaraciones aparecidas en los medios de comunicación que se utilizaron como fundamento para las sanciones. El multimillonario también posee activos en el sector de las telecomunicaciones, las empresas de Internet y los medios de comunicación, y es propietario del diario económico ruso "Kommersant". Los países de la UE suelen debatir la renovación de las sanciones a Rusia hasta el último momento, lo que en el pasado se debió en gran medida a las exigencias del antiguo líder húngaro, Viktor Orbán, y de Eslovaquia, que mantiene mejores relaciones con Moscú que la mayoría de los demás Estados de la UE. En junio, los países de la UE acordaron por primera vez prorrogar durante un año las sanciones sectoriales del bloque, como las relativas al sector energético, para reducir la posibilidad de que se produzcan esos debates.

item.title: Swiss upper house of parliament backs Mercosur trade deal
item.description: Switzerland's upper house of parliament approved a trade agreement with the South American bloc Mercosur on Monday after promising support for Swiss farmers, sending the deal back to the lower chamber, where it was rejected in June.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Switzerland's upper house of parliament approved a trade [USN:L1N3SY13X TEXT:"agreement"] with the South American bloc Mercosur on Monday after promising support for Swiss farmers, sending the deal back to the lower chamber, where it was [USN:L8N42Q06C TEXT:"rejected"] in June. A year after the Swiss economy minister signed the deal in Brazil, upper house lawmakers passed the accord coupled with financial aid for farmers worth 517 million Swiss francs ($633 million) over six years to cushion its impact. The deal between member states of the European Free Trade Association, or EFTA, and the core Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay passed with 35 votes in favour and seven against. There were three abstentions. Farming is a sensitive policy area in Switzerland and opposition to the agreement in the lower house this summer had come from both the right and left of the political spectrum. Switzerland is the biggest economy in EFTA, which also comprises Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. ($1 = 0.8162 Swiss francs)

item.title: Ukraine will support energy ceasefire if US ensures Moscow's intent, Zelenskiy says
item.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support a U.S. proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy sites only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war on Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support a U.S. proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy sites only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war on Ukraine. Zelenskiy made his comments in his nightly video address after U.S. President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed not to hit each other's energy [USN:FWN4560K2 TEXT:"targets"]. "If this can become the first de-escalatory step, a step towards ending Russian strikes against our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response, Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation," Zelenskiy said. "So far, no one has seen any genuine willingness on Russia's part to bring the war to an end. But if our American partners can secure Russia's genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps." In its 4-1/2-year-long war, Russia has often struck Ukrainian energy sites, a campaign that has caused major damage to heating and power networks and severely disrupted both industry and the daily lives of civilians. Ukraine's military has for months launched its own attacks on Russian industrial sites, particularly Russia's oil industry, a mainstay of the national economy. Those attacks caused serious shortages of petrol in many Russian regions. Zelenskiy posted comments earlier on social media that amounted to a denial that Ukraine had formally endorsed Trump's statement that both sides had agreed to halt attacks. The Ukrainian president said Ukraine was not convinced that Russia was willing to abide by any agreement. Any accord had to be "reliable, long-term, and actually have a real impact on people's lives", he said. In his statement, Trump said the two sides had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets. "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" he wrote on social media.

item.title: Verizon Wireless, T-Mobile resolve lawsuits over ad campaigns
item.description: Verizon Wireless and T-Mobile have resolved lawsuits accusing each other of deceiving consumers through ads that promised big savings from switching cellphone carriers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Verizon Wireless (VZ.N) and T-Mobile (TMUS.O) have resolved lawsuits accusing each other of deceiving consumers through ads that promised big savings from switching cellphone carriers. A stipulation of dismissal of Verizon's lawsuit and T-Mobile's countersuit was filed on Friday in Manhattan federal court. The dismissal came more than five months after U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan [USN:L6N40I1AF TEXT:"issued"] a preliminary injunction in Verizon's favor to block T-Mobile's "Save Over $1,000" campaign. Verizon, T-Mobile and their respective lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday. Settlement talks had included a possible framework to resolve similar future advertising-related disputes. Verizon sued T-Mobile in February. It later added claims that T-Mobile ads misled customers by promising more than $3,700 of savings over five years compared with Verizon and AT&T (T.N) , and promising to "save up to 20% vs. the other big guys." T-Mobile's [USN:L6N3ZQ0WH TEXT:"countersuit"] said Verizon's own campaign featuring bug-eyed images of George Washington, Abraham Lincoln and Benjamin Franklin was bogus because that carrier could not promise customers a "better deal." As of June 30, Verizon had 147 million subscribers according to its latest quarterly financial report. T-Mobile had slightly fewer subscribers before changing its disclosures of subscriber metrics this year.

item.title: AI apocalypse proves easier to ignore than price
item.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged labs to slow down before chatbots spiral out of control. It turbocharges a vibe shift ahead of his company's planned $2 trln IPO. Unlike the Cuban Missile Crisis or Covid-19's acute phase, investors are largely unfazed by theoretical tech risks.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Guilford
item.content:encoded: It’s a rare issue these days that unites avowed enemies like Elon Musk and Sam Altman. The bosses of SpaceX (SPCX.O) and OpenAI, respectively, endorsed warnings from their mutual rival Dario Amodei about the escalating threat from influential chatbots all three are developing. Anthropic's CEO added to the apocalyptic vibes, following widespread concerns about AI agents escaping confinement, with a long essay urging the industry to slow down before the technology spirals out of control. Discounting doomsday, however, is proving difficult. Advocating for a slowdown is heretical in Silicon Valley, especially from a founder like Amodei who's teeing up a $2 trillion [USN:L6N45316U TEXT:"initial public offering"]. His memo calls for empowering “third-party” investigators to verify that companies are pacing appropriately and assessing safety. He also wants labs in certain countries to form an alliance and governments worldwide to sign a compact promising restraint. Dismissive responses from President [USN:FWN4560E8 TEXT:"Donald Trump"] and China’s state-backed [USN:L4N45603J TEXT:"Global Times"] suggest international accord is unlikely. Musk, Altman and Amodei can, however, effect big shifts on their own. The shift in tone from breakneck advancement to a measured deceleration has vexed investors. The DRAM ETF, which tracks makers of the memory semiconductors that AI models devour, dropped by 7% and the chipmaking benchmark SOXX also dipped 5%. Server farm operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) is vulnerable, according to Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei, because much of its backlog is suited to training activity that presumably would slow. Its shares tipped about 6% lower. These sorts of moves are hardly unusual, however. CoreWeave’s amounts to roughly one standard deviation over the past year. The DRAM ETF drop is nothing like its double-digit tumbles back in June. Moreover, the VIX index, which measures anticipated volatility, jumped 5% on Monday, but remains sanguine, trading below 17, compared to 90 in October 2008 when financial Armageddon loomed. Training machines saps profitability, meaning investors might just welcome a slowdown. By contrast, Anthropic’s heavily adjusted gross margin, which mostly seems to measure this “inference” expense, surpassed 80%, according to the Financial Times . Moreover, an ever-widening series of hacks by OpenAI bots don’t seem to be stoking expectations of society-altering intervention. Ominous-sounding events have had an impact before. Covid-19 initially sent the S&P 500 Index plummeting 34%, reflecting greater sensitivity to infection counts than to deaths, academic researcher Badar Nadeem Ashraf found . Similarly, stocks took a hit during the early part of the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, if somewhat more mildly than might be expected for a looming nuclear war. It's easier, perhaps, to ignore an existential threat when it's theoretical than to put a price on it. Follow Jonathan Guilford on X and LinkedIn . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on September 12 entitled, "We must pace the frontier," calling on the AI industry to slow the rate at which it is improving the capabilities of new models. Elon Musk and Sam Altman, the respective bosses of SpaceX and OpenAI, both said in posts on X the same day that they agree with Amodei's proposals. President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post on September 14 that the only AI "guardrails" needed are a "strong and smart" president. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: US senators weigh requiring AI giants to commit to preventing catastrophe
item.description: U.S. Senate negotiators are debating legislation that would require AI companies to demonstrate they are taking reasonable precautions to keep their tools from causing harm, according to a Senate aide and a lobbyist familiar with the talks.
item.dc:creator: Courtney Rozen
item.content:encoded: U.S. Senate negotiators are debating legislation that would require AI companies to demonstrate they are taking reasonable precautions to keep their tools from causing harm, according to a Senate aide and a lobbyist familiar with the talks. Alarm about the potential danger posed by AI grew last week after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said he had resigned, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." AI-related stocks [USN:L6N45604K TEXT:"fell"] worldwide on Monday after leaders of some of the industry's largest companies called for slowing the pace of the technology's development. The senators are debating giving the U.S. commerce secretary the power to request proof that AI developers are taking reasonable steps to prevent harm, known as a "duty of care," according to the Senate aide and lobbyist. The secretary would also have the power to deploy government auditors to test companies' products themselves, they said. Reuters could not immediately determine what would qualify as “reasonable.” The legislation is still being debated. Even if Congress approves the measure, it faces long odds of becoming law. U.S. President Donald Trump [USN:FWN4560E8 TEXT:"said"] on Monday that existing authorities already provide adequate tools to regulate and prosecute tech companies, suggesting he wouldn't sign a bill setting new rules for AI. The proposal is being discussed by Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz and Senator Amy Klobuchar, the top Democrat involved in the negotiations. A spokesperson for Cruz did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters. "There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race," Thune told reporters on Monday. "I’m continuing to work toward a bipartisan agreement on legislation for government oversight of the greatest risks posed by AI models," Klobuchar said in a statement. "That includes requiring developers to work with government experts to verify and test models to make sure AI is safe." Cruz's Senate committee has oversight of the U.S. Commerce Department, the agency with in-house AI safety researchers. Senator Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Commerce Committee, has also weighed in on the legislation, sources say. Reuters [USN:L6N4530YF TEXT:"reported"] on Friday that negotiators are also debating involving federal courts if the U.S. government wants to block the release of certain AI models that it deems unsafe. Companies would be able to challenge that decision in federal court, and the exact structure of how much power the U.S. government would have is still being discussed. Part of the measure involving federal courts would also block states from enforcing their own laws governing certain risks posed by AI models, according to another lobbyist and a Senate aide. The U.S. companies known for the most advanced AI models are Anthropic and OpenAI.

item.title: Vista Equity exploring strategic options for financial software provider Finastra, sources say
item.description: Private equity firm Vista Equity Partners is exploring strategic options for Finastra which could include a potential sale of the software provider focused on financial institutions, four people familiar with the matter said.
item.dc:creator: Amy-Jo Crowley, Milana Vinn
item.content:encoded: Private equity firm Vista Equity Partners is exploring strategic options for Finastra which could include a potential sale of the software provider focused on financial institutions, four people familiar with the matter said. The buyout group is working with investment bankers at Morgan Stanley (MS.N) on the process, which is in its early stages and could include a full sale of the company but also may result in Vista divesting a stake or Finastra merging with or acquiring another industry player, said the sources. Finastra has already attracted initial interest from parties including other investment firms, the sources said. Blackstone (BX.N) is among prospective bidders studying the company, one of the sources added. The sources cautioned there was no certainty the process will result in a transaction, and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations. Vista, Finastra, Morgan Stanley and Blackstone all declined to comment. Vista is seeking to capitalize on renewed investor interest in financial software assets, even as valuations in the sector continue to struggle amid uncertainty over how artificial intelligence could disrupt business models and profitability. Two of the people said Finastra could be valued at more than high-single-digit billion dollars, while a third person said traditional earnings multiples for a specialized software company would value Finastra as high as $12 billion. The company expects to generate earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization of $650 million this year, the third source said. London-headquartered Finastra provides software used by banks and other financial institutions for payments, lending, and corporate banking operations. The company was formed in 2017 by Vista through the combination of Misys and Canada's D+H and serves thousands of financial institutions globally, including more than 80% of the world's top banks, according to its website. The business has undergone a significant transformation since Chris Walters was appointed chief executive in January 2025, with units shed to better focus on its core competencies of payments and lending software. This included selling Finastra’s treasury and capital markets business to buyout firm Apax Partners, which was rebranded as Teciem upon completion of the deal in February. Finastra also agreed in June to sell its [USN:L6N42R0KX TEXT:"universal banking business"] to Pollen Street Capital.

item.title: Winter is coming: airBaltic debt woes herald tough season ahead for smaller airlines
item.description: After Latvian airline airBaltic filed Chapter 11 proceedings on Monday, the aviation sector is bracing for a tough winter as the Iran war continues to push up jet fuel costs.
item.dc:creator: Joanna Plucinska, Gianluca Lo Nostro
item.content:encoded: After Latvian airline airBaltic filed [USN:L6N4560BF TEXT:"Chapter 11 proceedings"] on Monday, the aviation sector is bracing for a tough winter as the Iran war continues to push up jet fuel costs. The U.S. war with Iran has sparked the worst airline crisis in terms of costs since the COVID-19 pandemic, and airBaltic became the first European carrier during the conflict to file for bankruptcy, while U.S. peer Spirit [USN:L4N41E16Z TEXT:"collapsed"] in May after seeking protection before the war. Airlines operate with relatively thin margins compared to other sectors, leaving them more [USN:L6N4390PU TEXT:"exposed"] to geopolitical turmoil, particularly in winter when they burn through cash they earned in the busy summer season as bookings and travel slow. SACRIFICING RETURNS Smaller carriers are particularly vulnerable to further earnings pressure, with the price of jet fuel set to stay high as long as the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked. "Smaller, niche players are (most) at risk," aviation analyst John Strickland said. Bigger budget airlines that depend on offering cheap fares are also being hit hard by a doubling of fuel prices since the war began in late February, although they also have individual strengths. Wizz Air's (WIZZ.L) operating losses [USN:L6N4430FC TEXT:"deepened"] in the first quarter, it reported last month, saying it expects revenue per seat to keep falling in the current quarter after it cut fares to attract passengers. They reached a record 8.7 million in August. "Supported by strong liquidity, a disciplined hedging programme and one of Europe’s youngest and most efficient fleets, Wizz Air continues to invest, grow and serve more customers than ever,” the airline said in a statement to Reuters on Monday. James Halstead, managing partner at Aviation Strategy, said that Wizz Air is in a better position than state-owned airlines thanks to its stock market listing. "They are growing strongly, which means they are sacrificing returns now for future stability. They have a very good brand and operating model and they do have support," he said. Elsewhere, Southeast Asian budget carrier [USN:L8N44U0IG TEXT:"AirAsia"] (AIRG.KL) is seeking to raise fresh capital after consistent losses and an aggressive restructuring, while Canada's Air Transat has struggled with spiralling jet fuel costs. AirAsia said it saw no problems with its business sustainability and was seeing strong underlying demand. "AirAsia remains focused on maintaining business continuity and stable operations across all its markets and we continue to see strong underlying demand across our network," AirAsia said in a statement. "We are also working closely with our stakeholders to manage our financial and operational requirements." Air Transat did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. MORE ROUTES FOR BIGGER PLAYERS A tough market could see some smaller national airlines cede routes to larger, deeper-pocketed rivals, executives and investors said. They could also face challenges from budget airlines such as Ryanair (RYA.I) and Wizz Air that have taken over smaller secondary airports and worked to take plum slots and routes across central Europe in a push for growth - offering consumers better price options, analysts say. In August, Wizz Air CEO Jozsef Varadi told reporters that the carrier was keen to take over routes from Romania's state-backed carrier TAROM. TAROM did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The tougher market conditions could accelerate a long-standing move in Europe towards consolidation, pushing some smaller carriers into bigger groups like British Airways-owner IAG (ICAG.L) , Lufthansa (LHAG.DE) and Air France-KLM (AIRF.PA) . Norse Atlantic (NORSE.OL) , which is still reporting quarterly losses, in July [USN:L6N43X17W TEXT:"started"] a process for a sale or merger. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Poland's state-owned carrier LOT has been a suspected consolidation target for years. LOT did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AirBaltic has said it is looking for another strategic investor, but none has publicly expressed interest to date. Lufthansa owns a 10% stake in airBaltic but has said it doesn't plan to increase its stake. It declined to comment on what its next steps could be given airBaltic's Chapter 11 proceedings. Still, analysts said Chapter 11 proceedings could give airBaltic the chance to recover and survive, unlike Spirit. "This gives them a protective framework to put their house in order," said Strickland, pointing to Scandinavian rival SAS as a successful example of a turnaround.

item.title: Law firm Morgan & Morgan touts $1 billion AI investment, plans to sell platform to other firms
item.description: Morgan & Morgan, which bills itself as the largest U.S. personal injury law firm, said on Monday that it has committed to investing at least $1 billion into AI and technology over the next decade and will begin marketing its own AI platform to other law firms next year.
item.dc:creator: Sara Merken
item.content:encoded: Morgan & Morgan, which bills itself as the largest U.S. personal injury law firm, said on Monday that it has committed to investing at least $1 billion into AI and technology over the next decade and will begin marketing its own AI platform to other law firms next year. The Orlando, Florida-based firm said it already spent $300 million building its AI platform, called MX2, which it said it uses to extract medical information, generate case documents and prepare for trials. It said the platform now has nearly 5,000 monthly users. The investment will include hiring personnel and building new software and security capabilities, Yath Ithayakumar, the firm's chief transformation officer, said in an interview. The majority "is going to be very targeted towards AI," he said. The announcement comes as major corporate defense law firms are also investing heavily in AI. Kirkland & Ellis said in May that it is [USN:L6N4251D3 TEXT:"devoting $500 million"] of its revenue to developing a custom AI platform over the next three to four years. Other law firms have inked agreements with major technology companies to jointly create AI tools. London-based Freshfields said in April it will work with the legal team at Anthropic, the maker of Claude, to [USN:L6N41615T TEXT:"develop AI applications"] for legal services. Reuters' parent company Thomson Reuters also sells AI-assisted tools for the legal industry. Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan said in a statement that his firm, with more than 1,100 lawyers, was ahead of its rivals in AI adoption and that trial-focused firms like his were more insulated than corporate firms from being replaced by the technology. "Firms which bill by the hour to draft and review agreements or read through thousands of pages of documents are the practices AI will replace – almost entirely," he said. The firm said it plans to make MX2 available to other law firms, including corporate and transactional practices, by the end of 2027 on an invitation-only basis. "We think we're in a great position to help law firms solve tough problems and we're confident we can do it," Ithayakumar said. The firm did not say how it would price access to the platform. Reuters had reported in June that Morgan & Morgan, which has [USN:L1N41J1L3 TEXT:"annual revenue of $2.4 billion"], had hired JPMorgan to explore a minority stake sale that could eventually make way for the firm to go public. Widespread AI adoption by lawyers is expected to speed their work, but it has also created problems when attorneys have relied on AI-generated results without checking their accuracy. A federal judge in Wyoming [USN:L2N3PG0KY TEXT:"sanctioned"] two lawyers from Morgan & Morgan last year for citing fake cases generated by AI in a court filing. Ithayakumar said the error in the case took place "because we were early adopters of AI and we were moving fast." He said the firm has invested in training processes to make it easier for lawyers and staff to review AI outputs.

item.title: Falcons DL Da'Shawn Hand out for season with torn quad
item.description: Atlanta Falcons defensive lineman Da'Shawn Hand is scheduled to undergo surgery for a torn quad muscle and will miss the remainder of the season, head coach Kevin Stefanski said Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Atlanta Falcons defensive lineman Da'Shawn Hand is scheduled to undergo surgery for a torn quad muscle and will miss the remainder of the season, head coach Kevin Stefanski said Monday. Hand, 30, played just seven defensive snaps and did not record a tackle in his Atlanta debut on Sunday, a 20-13 defeat on the road against the Pittsburgh Steelers. In 78 career games (26 starts), Hand has recorded 6.5 sacks, 131 tackles, four forced fumbles and one interception for the Detroit Lions (2018-21), Tennessee Titans (2021-22), Miami Dolphins (2023-24), Los Angeles Chargers (2025) and Falcons. Detroit drafted him in the fourth round in 2018. --Field Level Media

item.title: FDA holds public hearing on psychedelic drugs as Trump-driven push gathers pace
item.description: The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses.
item.dc:creator: Puyaan Singh, Kamal Choudhury
item.content:encoded: The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses. The hearing is part of a broader push launched in [USN:L6N41103Y TEXT:"April"], when Trump ordered the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to focus on qualifying psychedelic drug programs for its priority-voucher program. The order also directed the FDA to work with the Drug Enforcement Administration on a pathway for some patients to obtain investigational treatments under a law, which allows certain seriously ill patients to seek experimental therapies, and to increase collaboration with the Department of Veterans Affairs. Since then, the FDA has issued [USN:L4N4171B4 TEXT:"priority vouchers"] to three companies developing psychedelic-based treatments, one for psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, another for psilocybin for major depressive disorder and a third for methylone for post-traumatic stress disorder. The hearing focuses on practical issues that could shape how psychedelic therapies are tested and delivered, including provider training and credentials, patient screening and monitoring, access and reimbursement, clinic capacity and the collection of long-term safety data. The FDA said it was not seeking views on individual drug applications, the scheduling of controlled substances or the legalization of psychedelics. Doctors, veterans, pharmacists and therapists during the hearing urged the regulator to establish clear safety and access standards for psychedelic-assisted therapies. Experts said any approved psychedelic treatment must include trained staff in the room during sessions, along with proper screening, follow-up care and community support. Robert Barrow, CEO of Definium Therapeutics, which is developing an LSD-based therapy, told Reuters that the hearing offers "a nice opportunity for that continuing public dialogue" among regulators, clinicians and patients. He said regulators and industry should treat psychedelics "like it's normal drug development, normal science, normal medicine," rather than as an unusually novel category requiring special treatment. Just days before the hearing, senior FDA officials, including Michael Davis, head of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine outlining a framework for developing and approving psychedelic drugs and saying the agency was "meeting this moment" on hard-to-treat conditions such as major depressive disorder and PTSD. The American Psychiatric Association said it "appreciates the FDA's public hearing and coordination with federal partners on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelics." "The FDA's determination of safety and effectiveness... must remain the foundation for any future clinical use." Jefferies analysts said the framework suggested the FDA was willing to consider flexible trial designs to address challenges including "functional unblinding," when a drug's noticeable psychoactive effects reveal to participants which treatment they received. The administration's support has stirred fresh [USN:L4N41K0YB TEXT:"investor interest"] in the sector, with industry executives telling Reuters it could improve coordination between the FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration and help reduce regulatory delays, even as researchers noted that approved treatments were still likely years away. Continued alignment among regulators, clinicians and developers on a safe, supervised rollout should benefit AtaiBeckley , Compass Pathways (CMPS.O) , Definium Therapeutics (DFTX.O) , Helus Pharma (HELP.NLB) , and GH Research (GHRS.O) , analysts said. Helus CEO Michael Halstead said "the science continues to advance, and continued thoughtful engagement among regulators, researchers and clinicians is critical to advancing these promising new treatments."

item.title: India opens door to fees on large payments made via UPI system
item.description: India notified changes in its payments legislation on Monday, specifying that banks cannot impose charges on payments via Unified Payments Interface transactions of up to 2,000 rupees ($20.93).
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: India notified changes in its payments legislation on Monday, specifying that banks cannot impose charges on payments via Unified Payments Interface transactions of up to 2,000 rupees ($20.93). The notification altered an earlier provision that prevented banks from charging fees on digital payments via India's popular UPI, paving the way for charges to be imposed on larger transfers. A final decision on whether to introduce charges, and how they would be levied, has yet to be taken. Here are some details: UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, is the world's largest retail fast-payment system by transaction volume, according to a 2025 IMF report. The new rule keeps UPI payments of up to 2,000 rupees free of charges. It paves the way for banks and payment companies to charge on larger UPI payments. Any fee, if introduced, would be paid by merchants rather than consumers, government officials have previously said. Banks and payment service providers stand to benefit from a potential new revenue stream. Jefferies estimated in August that merchant fees on larger UPI transactions could generate 50 billion rupees to 100 billion rupees annually for the payments industry. UPI, launched a decade ago, processed 24.51 billion transactions worth 29.82 trillion rupees in August. Google Pay and Walmart's PhonePe accounted for about three-fourths of monthly transaction volumes. Payments made using debit cards on India's homegrown RuPay network will remain free. ($1 = 95.5500 Indian rupees)

item.title: German finance minister lays out demands to UniCredit CEO on possible Commerzbank takeover
item.description: German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil set out demands to UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel on Monday over the Italian bank's possible takeover of Commerzbank .
item.dc:creator: Christian Kraemer, Maria Martinez, Tom Sims, Valentina Za
item.content:encoded: German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil set out demands to UniCredit (CRDI.MI) CEO Andrea Orcel on Monday over the Italian bank's possible takeover of Commerzbank (CBKG.DE) . They included Commerzbank remaining listed on the stock exchange, keeping its base in Frankfurt and continuing to finance German medium-sized companies at home and abroad, the German ministry said in a statement. The meeting in Berlin marked a turning point in the two-year battle for control of one of Germany's biggest banks after Berlin failed in its attempt to stymie a takeover. "In a constructive discussion with Mr. Orcel, I made it clear that the further negotiations must be conducted responsibly," said Klingbeil. Orcel said in a statement that the meeting was a "good and constructive initial discussion, that will be swiftly followed by others." "It’s for both sides to now reflect on this initial discussion so that a way forward can be found in the best interest of all stakeholders and shareholders,” he said. Commerzbank declined to comment. After months of resistance, German government officials and Commerzbank executives softened their resistance to a potential deal after UniCredit amassed a stake of nearly 50%. Now German officials are hoping to protect jobs as well as the brand of a bank that plays a critical role in financing the medium-sized companies in Europe's largest economy, whose government is in the throes of a [USN:L8N44Z070 TEXT:"political crisis"]. "This is no longer just about a hostile takeover, but about finding the best path forward for both banks," a German finance ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday. A combination of UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion in assets across two of the euro zone's largest economies. Orcel pounced on Commerzbank in 2024, taking the lender and the government off guard by discreetly building up a holding. Commerzbank and Berlin tried to prevent the takeover, but [USN:L6N44O0X1 TEXT:"threw in the towel"] after UniCredit amassed a stake nearing 50%. The German government holds a 13.3% stake in Commerzbank following a bailout during the global financial crisis.

item.title: Abbott to pay $384 million over contaminated infant formula allegations, US Justice Dept says
item.description: Abbott Laboratories has agreed to pay more than $384 million to settle allegations it knowingly manufactured infant formula in environments that posed a substantial risk of contamination, then sold the products to federal and state programs, the U.S. Justice Department said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Abbott Laboratories has agreed to pay more than $384 million to settle allegations it knowingly manufactured infant formula in environments that posed a substantial risk of contamination, then sold the products to federal and state programs, the U.S. Justice Department said on Monday. The deal resolves claims Abbott knew the conditions and manufacturing processes at Abbott's Sturgis, Michigan, and Casa Grande, Arizona, formula production plants increased the risk of contamination, but failed to properly test the products or alert regulators to positive tests. Payments for the products came out of U.S. Department of Agriculture and Medicaid funds, according to the department. The USDA and state Medicaid funds are used to subsidize the costs of baby formula for eligible families. There was no finding of liability and the company did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement. The department closed a related criminal investigation, Abbott said in a statement. The lawsuit followed a 2022 recall of Abbott baby formula products after complaints they were contaminated with a potentially deadly bacteria. Abbott initiated a recall of its infant formula products and closed its Michigan plant in 2022 after investigators found traces of a potentially deadly bacteria at that plant. The recall and the plant closure worsened a national shortage of baby formula that had begun with pandemic supply chain issues. Abbott said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for the bacteria. "Nothing matters more than the safety and quality of Abbott's products," the company said. "We make infant formula with the same care we would for our own families and are deeply committed to earning and maintaining caregivers' trust."

item.title: US judge says she will stay on OpenAI case after divesting Microsoft stock
item.description: U.S. Magistrate Judge Ona Wang, who is overseeing pretrial issues in a landmark copyright lawsuit brought by authors and news outlets including the New York Times against OpenAI and its largest financial backer Microsoft , disclosed in a court filing in Manhattan on Friday that she owned Microsoft stock but would not recuse herself from the case.
item.dc:creator: Blake Brittain
item.content:encoded: U.S. Magistrate Judge Ona Wang, who is overseeing pretrial issues in a landmark copyright lawsuit brought by authors and news outlets including the New York Times (NYT.N) against OpenAI and its largest financial backer Microsoft (MSFT.O) , disclosed in a court filing in Manhattan on Friday that she owned Microsoft stock but would not recuse herself from the case. Wang said in the filing that while judicial rules would ordinarily require her to recuse, she had divested her interest in the company and that it had not impacted any of her decisions. The judge also said that continuing to oversee the case would be in the public interest in order to "avoid having the matter reassigned to another magistrate judge." Spokespeople for Microsoft, OpenAI and The New York Times did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the filing on Monday. A spokesperson for Wang's court, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, and an attorney for the authors declined to comment. The Times' lawsuit, first [USN:L1N3DM0O2 TEXT:"filed in 2023"], accuses OpenAI and Microsoft of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train ChatGPT. The authors, who include John Grisham, Jonathan Franzen and George R.R. Martin, [USN:L1N3AW1AA TEXT:"separately sued"] the companies the same year for using their books to train OpenAI's popular chatbot. Those cases and related lawsuits against OpenAI were [USN:L6N3QH0VL TEXT:"consolidated in New York"] last year. Dozens of [USN:L6N3XM122 TEXT:"other complaints"] have also been brought by copyright owners against tech companies over what they call the theft of their material to train AI systems. The case is In re OpenAI Inc Copyright Infringement Litigation, U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, No. 1:25-md-03143. For OpenAI: Andrew Gass of Latham & Watkins, Joseph Gratz of Morrison & Foerster, Robert Van Nest of Keker Van Nest & Peters For Microsoft: Annette Hurst of Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe For the authors: Justin Nelson of Susman Godfrey For the news outlets: Ian Crosby and Davida Brook of Susman Godfrey

item.title: Trump resta importancia a la alarma sobre la seguridad de la IA
item.description: El presidente Donald Trump dijo el lunes que Estados Unidos ya cuenta con medidas de control para regular y fiscalizar a las empresas de inteligencia artificial, con lo que parecía restar importancia a las preocupaciones expresadas por los líderes del sector durante el fin de semana sobre el uso indebido de la IA.
item.dc:creator: Katharine Jackson, Courtney Rozen
item.content:encoded: El presidente Donald Trump dijo el lunes que Estados Unidos ya cuenta con medidas de control para regular y fiscalizar a las empresas de inteligencia artificial, con lo que parecía restar importancia a las preocupaciones expresadas por los líderes del sector durante el fin de semana sobre el uso indebido de la IA. "El único control o 'medidas de seguridad' que necesita la IA es un PRESIDENTE FUERTE E INTELIGENTE (¡con un alto coeficiente intelectual!), y Estados Unidos lo tiene, ¡y de sobra!", escribió Trump en Truth Social, "¡Ya tenemos un enorme poder PENAL y REGULADOR sobre estas empresas! Se está gestando una conspiración ENFERMIZA contra la IA y los centros de datos, y el único que se alegra de ello es China". La alarma sobre el daño potencial de la IA creció la semana pasada cuando el investigador de Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, anunció que había dimitido y que "las personas que desarrollan la IA creen sinceramente que podría matarnos a todos antes de que termine la década". Las acciones relacionadas con la IA cayeron en picado en todo el mundo el lunes, después de que los jefes de algunas de las mayores empresas del sector pidieran que se frenara el ritmo de desarrollo de esta tecnología. El presidente ejecutivo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei, escribió en un artículo publicado el sábado que el Gobierno de Estados Unidos debería elaborar normativas que exijan auditorías independientes de las herramientas de IA más avanzadas, conocidas como modelos «de vanguardia». Esbozó un marco de tres pasos destinado a moderar el ritmo de desarrollo de la IA y disponer de más tiempo para gestionar sus riesgos. La propuesta fue respaldada de inmediato por varios otros ejecutivos de importantes empresas de IA, entre ellos Elon Musk, de xAI, y el presidente ejecutivo de OpenAI, Sam Altman. El vicepresidente JD Vance dijo el lunes a los periodistas que se muestra escéptico ante el hecho de que los directivos del sector de la IA pidan al Gobierno de Estados Unidos que regule el sector. "Me resulta un poco extraño que haya tantas empresas tecnológicas de IA de vanguardia que, en cierto modo, acudan al Gobierno y le supliquen que las regule", dijo Vance. El senador estadounidense Mark Warner, demócrata por Virginia y figura destacada en materia de legislación tecnológica, habló con Amodei y Altman durante el fin de semana sobre las preocupaciones relativas a la seguridad de la IA, informó su portavoz. Trump dijo que las herramientas destinadas a garantizar la seguridad de la IA ya se habían utilizado con Amodei. "La Administración Trump ha impedido que las 'personas' de la IA hagan 'cosas' malas, o potencialmente malas, como Dario (¡Anthropic!), que ahora finge ser un 'angelito perfecto', y seguiremos haciéndolo", escribió Trump en las redes sociales. El equipo de comunicación de Anthropic no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios de Reuters sobre la declaración de Trump. El presidente republicano se ha resistido a avivar las preocupaciones sobre la inteligencia artificial y, en su segundo mandato, ha apoyado en gran medida a las empresas de IA. Trump tiene previsto reunirse con el presidente chino, Xi Jinping, la próxima semana en Washington. Reuters ya había informado de que ambos países estaban planeando otra reunión a mediados de septiembre para debatir los riesgos de la IA, dirigida por funcionarios gubernamentales de menor rango.

item.title: States, cities sue to block Trump immigration rule on public benefits
item.description: Dozens of Democratic-led U.S. states, counties and cities sued President Donald Trump's administration on Monday to block a new rule that would allow immigration officials to deny green cards to people who use public benefits such as food stamps and Medicaid.
item.dc:creator: Nate Raymond
item.content:encoded: Dozens of Democratic-led U.S. states, counties and cities sued President Donald Trump 's administration on Monday to block a new rule that would allow immigration officials to deny green cards to people who use public benefits such as food stamps and Medicaid. In two lawsuits filed in Manhattan federal court, the states and local governments challenged a federal rule set to take effect on Friday that says people applying to become lawful permanent residents should not be "public charges" who are primarily dependent on government benefits. The Department of Homeland Security rule was [USN:L1N43I0VD TEXT:"announced in July"]. It revives a policy adopted in 2019 during the Republican president's first term in office that was abandoned under Democratic President Joe Biden's administration, which in 2022 adopted a narrower definition of who would be a "public charge." Asked about the lawsuits, a DHS spokesperson in a statement called the plaintiffs "sanctuary states" and "left-wing leaders" who were "terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs." Under U.S. law, immigration officials have long been allowed to deem people inadmissible if they determine they would likely become "public charges" who would primarily depend on the government for support. Under the [USN:L1N30F16I TEXT:"Biden-era rule"], immigration officials could consider immigrants' prior or current receipt of Supplemental Security Income and cash assistance but not their receipt of non-cash benefits such as food stamps and Medicaid, the government healthcare program for low-income people. Those non-cash benefits had been factors under the 2019 rule and may now be considered again under the new policy. The states argue there are no clear limits on which benefits could count against a green card applicant, leaving families guessing which forms of assistance could jeopardize their immigration status. "This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, healthcare coverage and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled," New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, said in a statement. Her state, along with California and Illinois, is leading a lawsuit by 22 states and the District of Columbia challenging the rule. A second case was filed by six cities and counties including New York City, Chicago, San Francisco and Seattle. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a statement said the rule "seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades." The lawsuits argue that the new rule violates a federal law called the Administrative Procedure Act because it exceeds DHS's statutory authority and departs from the longstanding meaning of the public charge provision established by Congress. Similar lawsuits led to [USN:L1N2II33B TEXT:"rulings against"] the prior rule the first Trump administration had adopted, and the Biden administration dropped the government's defense of the policy before adopting its own rule.

item.title: Exxon Mobil shuts down Joliet refinery after power outage
item.description: Exxon Mobil brought its 264,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery in Joliet, Illinois, offline after a power outage occurred on Sunday, the company said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Jao
item.content:encoded: Exxon Mobil (XOM.N) brought its 264,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery in Joliet, Illinois, offline after a power outage occurred on Sunday, the company said on Monday. The outage occurred at about 3:30 p.m. CT on Sunday and power was restored at around 7:00 p.m., according to a company statement. The outage triggered the refinery's safety flare and resulted in a shutdown. The company said it is assessing the refinery's status, and the cause of the incident remains under investigation. Units are being stabilized after the plant-wide shutdown, IIR Energy said in a note, adding the refinery is expected return to normal service by the end of this week. The Joliet refinery supplies key fuels to consumers in the U.S. Midwest. It can produce about 11 million gallons a day of gasoline and diesel fuel, according to the company website. The disruption comes amid a tight global fuel market. The Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have strained fuel supplies, while strong exports have further tightened domestic inventories. The U.S. national average price of diesel last week [USN:L6N4521A4 TEXT:"surpassed $6 a gallon"] for the first time ever. Any prolonged operational disruptions could exacerbate an already tight fuel market, sending prices even higher.

item.title: Wall Street cierra con baja tras caída de las acciones de chips por los llamados a frenar la IA
item.description: Wall Street cerró con una baja el lunes, golpeado por las pérdidas de Nvidia y otros fabricantes de chips, después de que altos ejecutivos de empresas estadounidenses de inteligencia artificial (IA) plantearon preocupaciones de seguridad y pidieron que se frene el ritmo de desarrollo de la tecnología.
item.dc:creator: Noel Randewich
item.content:encoded: Wall Street cerró con una baja el lunes, golpeado por las pérdidas de Nvidia y otros fabricantes de chips, después de que altos ejecutivos de empresas estadounidenses de inteligencia artificial (IA) plantearon preocupaciones de seguridad y pidieron que se frene el ritmo de desarrollo de la tecnología. Los inversionistas también se mostraron nerviosos después de que el rendimiento de referencia de los bonos del Tesoro a 10 años superó brevemente el 5%, por primera vez desde 2023, antes de la reunión de la Reserva Federal de esta semana. Se espera, en general, que el banco central estadounidense suba las tasas de interés. Las acciones relacionadas con la IA cayeron en todo el mundo después de que los responsables de Anthropic, OpenAI y xAI advirtieron de los riesgos derivados de un desarrollo rápido, la amenaza más grave hasta la fecha para los miles de millones de dólares que se están invirtiendo en el sector y que han llevado a los mercados a máximos históricos. Las acciones de Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) , Micron Technology (MU.O) y Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O) bajaron, y el índice de chips PHLX (.SOX) cerró con una fuerte caída. Los futuros del crudo Brent cerraron con un alza del 1%, a 105,68 dólares por barril, a medida que aumentaba la preocupación por el suministro petrolero tras los nuevos ataques contra la infraestructura energética de Arabia Saudita y contra buques en Oriente Medio. La alta inflación, el fuerte endeudamiento de las empresas y del Gobierno, y las preocupaciones sobre la trayectoria fiscal a largo plazo de Estados Unidos han provocado un aumento de los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense durante el último mes. La cota del 5% que alcanzó el lunes el rendimiento a 10 años es un umbral que, según analistas, podría tener repercusiones en la economía estadounidense y mermar el atractivo de la renta variable estadounidense. Según el FedWatch de CME, los operadores están descontando una probabilidad del 90% de que la Fed suba las tasas de interés 25 puntos básicos en su reunión de política monetaria del miércoles. "Que el rendimiento a 10 años supere el 5% es algo enorme y lo dice todo, y puede presionar a la Fed para que haga algo más que una simple subida de tasas", dijo Jake Dollarhide, director ejecutivo de Longbow Asset Management. Según datos preliminares, el S&P 500 (.SPX) perdió 36,93 puntos, o un 0,48%, a 7.620,05 unidades, mientras que el Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) cedió 145,25 puntos, o un 0,55%, a 26.187,79. El Promedio Industrial Dow Jones (.DJI) cayó 151,66 puntos, o un 0,29%, a 52.421,63 unidades.

item.title: Trump calls $5,000 payouts 'easy' to fit into federal budget
item.description: President Donald Trump said the United States can afford his promise to send cash to every U.S. adult should the Republican Party keep control of Congress in this year's elections.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Chuck Mikolajczak, Padraic Halpin
item.content:encoded: (This Sept 13 story has been corrected to fix Mallory McMorrow's title in paragraph 6, and to fix the debt figure in Lawler's quote to '$40 trillion,' not '$4 trillion,' in paragraph 10.) President Donald Trump said on Sunday the United States can afford his promise to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult should his Republican Party keep control of Congress in this year's elections. "I don't know but it's easy if the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," Trump told reporters when asked if Congress would need to approve the payments, adding that trillions of dollars were coming into the country. Trump unveiled the idea of $5,000 payouts [USN:L1N451146 TEXT:"during a speech"] at the Republican Party convention last week. Speaking to reporters on Sunday in Ireland, where he was attending a golf tournament at his club in Doonbeg, the president said the U.S. government has the funds to pay for it. But any such payment would need to be approved by Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said on Sunday. "Of course, the devil's in the details. We have to figure all that out," Johnson told CNN's "State of the Union." Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talk shows panned the idea, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC's "This Week" that it is not a "serious proposal." Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, citing [USN:L1N41O16Y TEXT:"the elimination of some Affordable Care Act subsidies"], cast doubt on whether the promised $5,000 checks would be sent even if Republicans retain control of Congress. "There was an ACA subsidy cancellation," McMorrow, a Democrat, said on CNN. "I think it was $1,000 we were supposed to get. So if you believe that you're going to get $5,000, I've got a bridge to sell you." U.S. Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican in a closely contested race, would not specifically commit to Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal on Sunday. “I support putting money back in the pockets of hardworking Americans,” he said on ABC’s “This Week,” citing tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill that Republicans passed last year. “But whether you call it a stimulus check or a dividend, the question is, how do you pay for it? That's my focus. We have a $40 trillion debt, and we have to be serious about tackling that.” Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer watchdog Public Citizen, earlier called the move an attempt to buy votes. "This explicit and desperate attempt to buy votes in the November election is a new low. Trump knows he can’t do this, and yet he’s attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election, which is antithetical to every principle of American democracy."

item.title: US EPA to undo carbon emission limits for power plants at G20 meeting
item.description: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Monday announced rules to repeal former President Joe Biden's limits on carbon emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants and to prevent future climate-focused regulations of those facilities.
item.dc:creator: Valerie Volcovici, Georgina Mccartney, Ernest Scheyder
item.content:encoded: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Monday announced rules to repeal former President Joe Biden's limits on carbon emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants and to prevent future climate-focused regulations of those facilities. The move is part of President Donald Trump's efforts to unwind U.S. climate policy that his administration says has hindered energy production. The announcement was made on the sidelines of a gathering of G20 energy ministers this week in Houston, where the global officials will discuss energy security, expanding baseload power and "regulatory efficiency." EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said new moves to prevent future regulation of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector will enable the U.S. to build new generating infrastructure needed to meet skyrocketing electricity demand. "Americans have been demanding more common sense at federal agencies under President Trump's leadership," he said at a press conference in Houston. "That means cutting red tape so we can build new power-generating infrastructure." Environmental groups slammed the new proposal, saying it would cost more than that in damage to the environment and public health. The electricity sector is responsible for nearly a quarter of U.S. greenhouse gas pollution. Last June, Trump's administration issued its proposal to repeal rules written under Biden to curb emissions of carbon dioxide, mercury and other air pollutants from power plants. Biden's carbon emission rules for power plants would have reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 1 billion metric tons by 2047, part of his administration's fight against climate change. The rule would have required coal-fired power plants and new natural gas-fired generators to install equipment in the coming decade to capture emissions before they reach the atmosphere. That requirement made zero-emissions alternatives like solar and wind more attractive. "Denying the existence of a quarter of the country’s climate pollution is utterly reckless.
